message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Specialized for highly parallel tasks – originally for rendering graphics, now also used for scientific computing, machine learning, etc. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32), each very powerful with deep pipelines, large caches, complex control logic. | Thousands of smaller, simpler cores optimized for throughput rather than single‑thread performance. |
| **Instruction Set** | Complex instruction set architecture (CISC) or reduced instruction set (RISC) with sophisticated branching, caching, and out‑of‑order execution. | Very simple instruction set; many cores execute the same instruction on different data (SIMD). |
| **Memory Hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, high bandwidth memory access, sophisticated prefetchers. | Smaller per‑core cache, relies heavily on shared global memory; uses memory coalescing to maximize bandwidth. |
| **Parallelism** | Parallelism is limited by the number of cores and hyper‑threading; good at serial and irregular workloads. | Massive data‑parallelism; excels when the same operation can be applied to many independent data elements. |
| **Typical Workloads** | Control‑heavy tasks, branching, I/O, small data sets, real‑time responsiveness. | Data‑parallel tasks like matrix multiplication, convolution, image processing, physics simulations, AI inference/training. |
| **Power & Heat** | Designed for low power consumption per core; efficient for general use. | Higher raw compute power but often higher power draw; efficiency comes from parallelism. |
| **Programming Model** | Single‑threaded code runs fast; multi‑threading requires careful synchronization. | Requires writing kernels that run across many threads; programming models include CUDA, OpenCL, Vulkan, Metal. |

In short, a CPU is a versatile “master” processor that can handle a wide variety of tasks quickly, while a GPU is a specialized “worker” that can perform the same operation on thousands of data points simultaneously, making it ideal for workloads that can be expressed in a massively parallel way.
